title: Ramana's Forty Verses
hook: meant to be, or you made it happen?
tomorrow: a ring falls down a well. calling its name won't help. so?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana's Forty Verses: many ornaments, one gold, and knowing the knower. Today, an old quarrel with two sides.

Meant to be, or you made it happen? Both get said at graduation parties, sometimes by the same aunt in the same hour. Hindu thought has voices for both. Some stress what's already in motion, karma from before, now bearing fruit. Others stress effort, what a person does today. Ramana gives the quarrel one verse.
screen: `MEANT TO BE?` → `OR YOU MADE IT HAPPEN?` → `ONE VERSE FOR AN OLD QUARREL.`

segments.voice: First, the case for fate. Not everything that happens to a person was chosen this morning. Seeds planted long ago come up. That view brings humility, and it lets someone stop blaming themselves for what they couldn't control. Then the case for effort. Nothing grows without work. Whatever came before, the next step is still taken now, and that view won't let anyone give up. Here's Ramana's verse, in paraphrase: the argument over which wins, fate or free will, belongs only to those who don't know the root of both. Those who know the self, the root of fate and effort alike, are free of both. Look at the move. Both sides assume a doer in the middle, a karta, pushed by fate or pushing back. Ramana asks about the doer. Near the poem's end he says: if we are the doers, we'll taste the fruit. But when, by asking who the doer is, the self is known, the sense of being the doer drops, and with it all three kinds of karma. That isn't permission to sit on the couch. Plans still get made. What the verse questions is the little owner behind each act who says: mine.
screen: `THE CASE FOR FATE.` · `THE CASE FOR EFFORT.` · `BOTH ASSUME A DOER.` · `ASK WHO THE DOER IS.` · then, large: `NOT FATE, NOT EFFORT: WHO?`

segments.voice: Do one small thing within reach: straighten a cup, close a drawer, fold the corner of a blanket. Do it slowly. For the rest of the sit, watch for the thought that says I did that, and ask, gently, who.
Ramana's Forty Verses: a poem that meets the fate-or-effort quarrel by asking who the doer is.
Pocket this: Ramana's Forty Verses: not fate, not effort, but the one who's asking which. Rest well tonight.

notes: Debate shape: fate and effort each get their best case in the teach; the fork asks the learner to state the other side's best case. Answers 1689's question. Practice kind: do one small act. Surprising fact: the verse says the quarrel belongs only to those who don't know the root of both.
'Hindu thought has voices for both' (daiva and purushartha, e.g. Yoga Vasishtha stresses effort): kept general. 'Three kinds of karma' is in verse 38. Confirm.
